$comment: The build recipe as DATA — what to install and what to run, per platform and per accelerator.
Why a file and not an endpoint: this is needed BEFORE any sidecar exists. The whole distribution story
is that the customer's machine builds the flavour it needs (the execution provider is a compile-time
feature and the vendor providers may never be redistributed), so the thing that drives that build cannot
be served by the thing being built. It is checked into the repository and read from a checkout.
Why JSON and not TOML: it parses with serde_json, already a dependency here, and natively on the .NET
side that consumes it. No new package on either end.
The RAG side detects the card and picks a row; a human reading the same rows gets the same answer. That
is the requirement, and it is why every field is spelled for both readers rather than encoded.
`build_minutes` is MEASURED where it is present and ABSENT where nobody has measured it — the CUDA and
MIGraphX rows carry no number because building them needs a vendor toolchain this machine does not
have, and a guess would be worse than nothing: it is the field an operator uses to decide whether to
start a build now or after lunch. `build_minutes_measured` says on what, and when.
The tests in src/recipes.rs keep the feature flags and the flavour names honest against Cargo.toml, so
this file cannot quietly stop describing the crate — including the reverse direction, a feature added
with no recipe, which is the half that rots without anyone noticing.

recipes.title: Windows · DirectML
recipes.accelerator: any DirectX 12 GPU — AMD, Intel or NVIDIA
toolchain: Visual Studio Build Tools with the C++ workload

onnxruntime.how: downloaded by the ort crate as a prebuilt Windows package

recipes.why_not_shipped: DirectML is a vendor-licensed Microsoft redistributable. One cached copy in a registry, an image layer or an offline bundle would make us a redistributor.
recipes.verify: GET /health → active_provider = "dml", provider_ready = true, self_check.verified = true

recipes.title: Windows · NVIDIA CUDA
toolchain: Visual Studio Build Tools with the C++ workload
NVIDIA CUDA runtime libraries and cuDNN, installed by the operator

onnxruntime.how: the same prebuilt Windows package as DirectML — both EPs come from it
onnxruntime.operator_action: the CUDA provider DLLs must sit BESIDE THE EXECUTABLE: onnxruntime_providers_shared.dll and onnxruntime_providers_cuda.dll. ONNX Runtime resolves them from the exe's directory, not from PATH.

recipes.why_not_shipped: The CUDA runtime and cuDNN are vendor-licensed under NVIDIA's EULA and SLA. cuDNN is the most commonly mis-shipped of the three because it arrives as a plain folder of DLLs.
recipes.verify: GET /health → active_provider = "cuda". A binary built without the ort/cuda feature registers no CUDA EP and answers 500 in ~4 ms while still reporting the REQUESTED provider — which is why requested, compiled and active are three separate fields.
recipes.known_trap: `--features cuda` still links DirectML, because both EPs come from one package. Seeing `-l DirectML` in the build log is therefore no evidence about CUDA either way. Read the feature tree, not the link line.

recipes.title: Linux / WSL · AMD ROCm via MIGraphX
toolchain: pkg-config and libssl-dev — on Linux fastembed's downloader links system OpenSSL; Windows uses Schannel and needs neither
an ONNX Runtime BUILT FROM SOURCE with --use_migraphx: no prebuilt package ships this EP

onnxruntime.how: built from source by the operator, from a tag satisfying ort's required API version
onnxruntime.operator_action: point ORT_DYLIB_PATH at the resulting libonnxruntime.so. It must be at least ONNX Runtime 1.x where x is ort::MINOR_VERSION; the sidecar preflights this at startup and exits naming both versions, because ort's own version check DEADLOCKS instead of erroring on a mismatch.
onnxruntime.also_required: ORT_MIGRAPHX_MODEL_CACHE_PATH must be set and writable. ROCm's MIGraphX EP always saves the compiled model, and with no path it writes to "" — the write fails and takes the kernel call with it, so every /embed answers 500 after a ~2-minute compile with the GPU idle.

recipes.why_not_shipped: The ONNX Runtime build is the operator's own, and nothing here bundles ROCm.
recipes.verify: GET /health → active_provider = "migraphx", adapter = null (DXGI is Windows-only, so the raw ORT_DEVICE_ID semantics apply)
recipes.known_trap: A separate --target-dir is not optional: the Windows and Linux flavours must never share target/, or each clobbers the other's artefacts.

recipes.title: CPU only
toolchain: a C++ toolchain for the platform (MSVC Build Tools on Windows, cc/pkg-config on Linux)

onnxruntime.how: downloaded by the ort crate as a prebuilt package

recipes.build_minutes_measured: 2026-08-19, cold release build with a warm cargo registry, Windows 11, x86_64: 4m29s. A cold registry adds the download of ~348 crates.
recipes.verify: GET /health → compiled_providers = ["cpu"], and every embed runs — slowly. This is the flavour that may be published as a release artefact, because it carries no vendor component at all.
recipes.known_trap: Roughly forty times slower than a GPU flavour on the same work. A silent CPU fallback is exactly the failure the verification gate exists to catch — self_check.verified answers the numbers, active_provider answers the hardware.
